#4806. Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an ‘urgent need for action’

Volkswagen has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.

“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.

VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.

As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo Reuters reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.

The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch will be delayed until closer to 2030.

It should be noted that they paid out dividends of 2.6 billion in August. Most of it went to 3 majority shareholders. But they used a clever accounting trick to delay the losses till now, just before talks with unions about pay.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.

The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.

While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.

Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.

#4805. Weeds or Medicine? What Our Elders Knew About Mental Health

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

I was a child the first time my grandmother sent me to a field near our apartment in Pittsburgh.

It was not a cute, manicured garden; it was a literal field, the kind of overgrown, sun-baked stretch of land that most people walked past without a second glance. She handed me a paper bag and pointed. Go pick dandelion greens. And don’t come back with just a little bit. She said it the way she said everything—with the quiet authority of someone who knew exactly what she was doing, even when you had no idea why.

I complained, as children do. But I picked the greens. I brought them home. She washed them, cooked them down into her collard greens, and set a plate in front of me, like she had just done something completely ordinary. She had. She had also just given me medicine. She just didn’t call it that. I had to eat every ounce of what she gave me and drink the pot liquor (likker).

Our elders didn’t use the phrase gut-brain axis. They never read a study on psychobiotics or prebiotic fiber and mental health outcomes in adolescents. But they knew, in the way many Black elders just know things, through generations of accumulated wisdom passed down person to person, that what you put in your body changes how you feel, how you think, how you move through the world. They knew that food was not just fuel. It was healing. They knew food is medicine. And they made sure we got our portion of it, whether we wanted to go pick it or not. How many of you grew up forcing down the liver and onions your grandmother made you eat?

That weed in the field is not a weed. Dandelion has been used as medicine across cultures for centuries in West African herbal traditions, in Chinese medicine, in indigenous North American practice, in European folk healing. Enslaved Africans arriving in the American South recognized dandelion growing wild in the fields and incorporated it into their healing practices, just as they braided seeds into their hair and carried botanical knowledge across the Middle Passage. According to the Black Food Canon, dandelion was gathered as a field green across the South, wilted in pot likker, and used medicinally as a liver-supporting, digestion-stimulating bitter. It was not a weed. It was part of a pharmacy growing at the edge of the yard. There are so many others, including red clover and plantain.

Modern science has confirmed what our ancestors practiced. Dandelion greens are rich in prebiotic fiber, the kind that feeds beneficial bacteria in the gut, as well as vitamins A, C, and K; iron; calcium; and potent antioxidants. They support liver function, reduce inflammation, and improve gut motility. But here is the connection our elders did not state, but our generation needs to hear: A healthy gut is the foundation of a healthy mind.

The gut is the second brain. The gut-brain axis is one of the most rapidly advancing areas in mental health science. Researchers describe it as a bidirectional communication network linking the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system through the vagus nerve, neurotransmitters, immune signals, and microbial metabolites. In plain language, your gut and your brain are in constant conversation. The health of one shapes the health of the other. The gut microbiome, the ecosystem of bacteria living in your digestive system, turns out to be one of the most powerful influencers of mood, cognition, anxiety, and depression we have ever identified.

The implications for young people are especially significant. Research in Translational Psychiatry found that adolescence is a critical window when the gut-brain axis is actively being fine-tuned, meaning that dietary interventions during this period may produce long-lasting consequences for mental health, for better or worse. What a young person eats during adolescence is not just shaping their body; it is shaping their brain, their emotional regulation, and their resilience. Studies consistently show that gut microbiome disruption is associated with greater depression and anxiety symptoms in children and adolescents. And diets high in prebiotic fiber, the kind found in dandelion greens, collards, and the full range of foods that stocked Black Southern kitchens, are directly linked to improved mental health outcomes.

Our ancestors were doing precision mental health intervention; they just called it supper. The philosophy of food as medicine has deep roots in Black culture, stretching from West African food traditions through the survival kitchens of enslaved people to the Sunday dinner tables of the South. Enslaved Africans brought with them botanical knowledge—of roots, leaves, and herbs that sustained bodies and spirits through unimaginable conditions. Dark leafy greens, including collards, mustard greens, and dandelion, were used not just as sustenance but as tools of detoxification, immune support, and healing. The pot likker left behind after a slow cook of greens—that deeply concentrated, vitamin-rich broth that Black Southern grandmothers swore by—was medicine passed down in a pot.

Somewhere along the way, we began to see these traditions as old-fashioned, as poverty food, as things to leave behind on the way to modernity. We traded the field greens for processed food. We traded the slow-cooked pot for the fast-food drive-through. And our children, inheriting disrupted microbiomes and an unsupportive food system, are paying the price in their mental health.

I’m not saying a bowl of greens can replace clinical care, or that dandelion tea cures depression or a plate of collards replaces therapy. The youth mental health crisis demands systemic responses: more culturally affirming providers, better funding, greater access, and genuine investment in Black children’s well-being. But I am saying that we have underestimated how much damage we did when we walked away from the food traditions our elders built and how much healing is available to us if we walk back toward them. Nutritional psychiatry is now a recognized field. The research on diet and youth mental health is compelling and growing. Our elders were practicing it before it had a name.

Go pick some greens. The act of sending a child to the field is not just about the greens. It's about being in the earth, feeling the sun, bringing something back with your own hands that would feed the table. That act alone—the going outside, the bending down, the gathering, the returning—is the kind of embodied, nature-connected practice that research now tells us supports mental health in young people. Our elders were giving us prebiotic fiber, and they were giving us grounding. They were feeding our gut and our sense of belonging to something larger than ourselves.

#4804. The 89 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 16 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4803. The Unretirement Movement

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

More people of a certain age are holding jobs rather than waiting for their Social Security checks to arrive in the mail. The demographics of the American workforce are changing, and for the better, as it becomes more diverse in terms of age.

A 2026 AARP survey of adults age 50 and older found that over six months, 7 percent of retirees “unretired,” meaning they reentered the labor force. Not surprisingly, most of them reported that their primary reason for returning to work was to make money.

Financial problems most commonly push retirees back into the workforce: Spiraling healthcare costs or a health-related emergency are primary reasons that retirees return to work either part-time or full-time. Recent inflation spikes have also driven many older Americans to look for work, as the rising cost of living has reduced spending power. What might have seemed like a sizable nest egg has shrunk for many Americans, and the thought of running out of money is understandably terrifying.

Purpose, Structure, and Social Connection

Not just financial necessity but simply wanting to stay busy or engaged is behind the unretirement movement. While money is the major factor in returning to the workforce in some way, many retirees have found their post-career lives are not the nirvana they had expected. Americans as a whole have a strong work ethic, and full-time leisure is not as fulfilling or rewarding for those who have been productive for decades. Research indicates that engaging in work provides routine, purpose, and social connection, which can boost physical and mental well-being.

A growing labor shortage in many industries may help drive the unretirement movement and options for retirees who prefer to work on their own terms. Older adults are, among many other things, selling health insurance, becoming real estate agents, tutoring and substitute teaching, and working in retail or food service in their spare time.

Our knowledge economy also allows retirees to leverage the skills and wisdom they have gained over the years by serving as life coaches, youth mentors, community outreach specialists, and caregiving companions. According to Pivoters, which connects people over age 55 with employers looking for experienced talent, the United States has more than "100 million people 55 and over, most of whom need to work for financial reasons and want to work for the longevity, health, and social benefits of work.”

Baby boomers, now in their 60s and 70s, are not surprisingly leading the unretirement movement. In their book The Talent Revolution: Longevity and the Future of Work, Lisa Taylor and Fern Lebo examine the gradual sidelining of boomers in the American workforce. In the 1980s and 1990s, boomers were undoubtedly an economic powerhouse; however, a couple of decades later, society thinks they have little to contribute. The authors argue that digital technology created a false perception of this generation as obsolete—akin to viewing them as beta-max. The authors see older adults as essential to the future workplace, and longevity may pave the way for the coming “talent revolution.” “We identify boomers as revolutionaries—a population of disruptors that is altering career patterns, creating new expectations, and demanding inclusion,” they write.

Pairing Older Workers’ Wisdom with Younger Workers’

Chip Conley has conceived perhaps the most compelling and welcoming workplace scenario for older adults. The notion of modern elderhood has been simmering for some time, but Conley has shown how it could serve as a platform for age-friendly work. In his early 50s, Conley sold his business and wasn’t sure what to do next when he unexpectedly found a new gig as the designated “elder” for Airbnb, the online vacation rental marketplace. At that company, like most tech-driven ones, digital intelligence was the primary job qualification, putting young people with little managerial experience in major positions of power.

Conley wrote in his book Wisdom at Work, "Here exists a generation of older workers with invaluable skills—high emotional intelligence, good judgment born out of decades of experience, specialized knowledge, and a vast network of contacts—who could pair with these ambitious millennials to create businesses that are built to endure.” Conley advised older workers to repurpose their experience by seeking recognition as wise elders in organizations, like village elders in traditional societies who wielded authority based on the wisdom that came with age. Wise words indeed.

Conley, Chip. (2018). Wisdom at Work: The Making of a Modern Elder. New York: Crown Currency.

#4801. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4800. 100 Years of Pooh

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

A. A. Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh for his son, Christopher Robin. It was published on October 14, 1926, and sold 150,000 copies before the year was out. Pooh books have since sold more than 45 million copies in the United States alone, and have been translated into over 50 languages.

Milne was already a well-known humorist at Punch magazine and a successful playwright. Pooh himself made his first appearance in a London newspaper on Christmas Eve 1925.

Milne had served in the First World War, and Britain was still grieving. Into that world came a quiet forest where the biggest crisis was a lost tail or a bear stuck in a doorway. Pooh offered a refuge then, and he offers one now.

Part of the pleasure is knowing these characters so well. We can almost predict what each will say. Perhaps we recognize someone we love in many of them. Perhaps, we may even recognize ourselves.

Pooh's forgetfulness is a loose match for inattentive ADHD. He may lose track of a plan, especially when honey is involved, but he never loses his affection for a friend.

Piglet approaches life cautiously. His tendency to anticipate trouble resembles the worry of generalized anxiety disorder. Yet he is loyal and willing to help. He reminds us that bravery can come in a very small package, and that feeling afraid does not stop us from doing something meaningful.

Eeyore expects disappointment. His gloom brings to mind persistent depressive disorder. But his dry humor makes him much more than the sad member of the group. His friends keep including him. He does not have to become cheerful to deserve their attention.

Tigger is movement, excitement, and impulse, much like the hyperactive side of ADHD. He can be exhausting, but he brings vitality. Most of us know someone whose enthusiasm occasionally overwhelms us, and whose absence would leave the room noticeably quieter.

Rabbit likes order and likes to be in charge, which resembles obsessive-compulsive personality traits. Owl enjoys being the expert, a playful nod to narcissistic traits, though wanting to sound knowledgeable is hardly a personality disorder.

Little has changed in terms of human characteristics in 100 years.

Milne made a quietly radical choice for his time. In the Hundred Acre Wood, the child is the capable one. Christopher Robin solves problems, organizes expeditions, and reassures his anxious friends, while the animals around him are smaller and more muddled.

For young readers, this is empowering. Children spend most of their days being told what to do. In Pooh's world, they get to be the steady, kind, competent one. Perhaps that is why so many of us felt a little braver after reading these stories.

In 1953, the pediatrician and psychoanalyst D. W. Winnicott described what he called transitional objects: the beloved teddy bear or blanket that helps a young child move from total dependence toward independence. The object is comforting because it carries the feeling of being cared for even when a parent is out of the room.

Thirty years earlier, Milne took a transitional object and gave it a voice, a personality, and a whole forest. Every child who has hugged a stuffed animal at bedtime understands Pooh instinctively. In a sense, the books do for readers what the bear did for Christopher Robin. They offer comfort we can carry with us.

The friends keep making room for one another. They become annoyed. They misunderstand. Their efforts to help do not always go smoothly. These trials are what make their friendships believable.

Eeyore matters here. People with depression sometimes withdraw because they believe they will bring everyone else down. Friends, unsure what to say, may pull away too. The distance grows just when connection is needed most.

We can take a gentler approach: Keep inviting. Offer a walk, a cup of tea, or a little company. Allow room for quiet. In Pooh's world, a friend is someone worth checking on.

The Hundred Acre Wood offers a different pace. There is time to visit, walk, wonder, and become absorbed in something small. A modest adventure is enough to fill the day.

In 1982, Benjamin Hoff's bestseller The Tao of Pooh presented the bear as a model of simple, present-moment living. Long before mindfulness became a wellness trend, Pooh was savoring honey, noticing the weather, and enjoying his friends without needing to accomplish anything.

The word nostalgia was coined in 1688 by a Swiss physician who considered it a disease of homesick soldiers. Nostalgia tends to lift mood, strengthen our sense that life has meaning, and remind us that we are loved. In one study, people who felt lonely drew on nostalgic memories to restore their sense of connection. Looking back, it turns out, can help us move forward. The original stuffed animals that inspired Milne now live at the New York Public Library, where they receive 750,000 of visitors every year.

The last lesson, and it is a sober one. The real Christopher Robin did not always enjoy being famous. As he grew older, he was teased at school, and as an adult he wrote with mixed feelings about the boy in the books. His father eventually stopped writing about him, explaining that his son had "already had more publicity than I want for him."

These stories hold the wish to be known, accepted, and remembered. Near the end of The House at Pooh Corner, Christopher Robin asks Pooh to promise he won't forget him, "not even when I'm a hundred."

A century later, we have kept that promise too.

Hoff, B. (1982). The Tao of Pooh. Dutton.

Milne, A. A. (1926). Winnie-the-Pooh. Illustrations by E. H. Shepard. Methuen.

Milne, A. A. (1928). The House at Pooh Corner. Illustrations by E. H. Shepard. Methuen.

Milne, C. (1974). The Enchanted Places. Eyre Methuen.

#4798. Hyundai launches the new IONIQ 6 in the UK with up to 422 miles of range, starting at $45K

The new Hyundai IONIQ 6 is now on sale in the UK with an impressive range of up to 422 miles, starting at about $45,000.

Hyundai opened orders for the all-new IONIQ 6 in the UK, starting at £33,240 ($45,000), including the Electric Car Grant (ECG).

The “evolved” electrified streamliner brings a sharp new design, a refined interior, and a bigger battery for longer range.

Hyundai “enhanced every line and detail” for a cleaner, stronger silhouette. The front includes a redesigned shark nose and slim daytime running lights, while the black lower body garnish now extends into the doors.

The rear features a new extended ducktail design replacing the previous generation’s prominent spoiler.

Inside, Hyundai overhauled the new IONIQ 6’s interior with a redesigned two-tone leather steering wheel, a digital side mirror, and a “bridge-type” center console that includes a wireless phone charger and physical buttons.

It includes Hyundai’s new infotainment setup, including dual 12.3″ navigation and infotainment screens with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capabilities.

In the UK, the new IONIQ 6 is available in three trims: Premium, N-Line, and N-Line Evo, with 225 horsepower RWD or 320 horsepower AWD powertrains.

The base Hyundai IONIQ 6 Premium uses a new 84 kWh battery with the 225 hp RWD powertrain, delivering up to 422 miles of range and 4.6 miles/kWh efficiency.

It starts at £33,240 with the ECG. It includes 18″ alloy wheels, flush auto door handles, dual-zone climate control, heated front seats, heated steering wheel, heat pump, smart regenerative braking, wireless phone charging, over-the-air updates, and the full suite of key safety systems.

The IONIQ 6 N-Line starts at £36,240, including the ECG, and adds a more dynamic N-Line exterior and interior design.

Upgrading to the range-topping N-Line Evo costs £43,270 and adds features like leather and suede seat trim, a suede headliner, front relaxation seats, ventilated front seats, an electric sunroof, and a head-up display.

Other added features included with the N-Line Evo trim include Surround View Monitor, Remote Smart Parking Assist, Parking Collision Avoidance Assist, Digital Key 2, Walk-Away Lock, exterior Vehicle-to-Load adaptor, and BOSE premium audio.

Both the IONIQ 6 N-Line and N-Line Evo use the 84 kWh battery, providing up to 364 miles of driving range in RWD and up to 354 miles with the AWD powertrain.

Beautiful car, very efficient and from what I read, very comfortable. I had my eyes set on it, but the small trunk was a dealbreaker for me. So I went for the EV6, which is maybe even more of a stunner (in the eyes of the beholder) but admittedly significantly less efficient.

Thanks to its 800-volt electrical architecture, the IONIQ 6’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds of up to 350 kW.

The new IONIQ 6 is now available to order on Hyundai UK’s website, with deliveries set to begin in early 2027.

Sadly, those in the US will miss out on the new-and-improved electrified streamliner. Hyundai is discontinuing the standard IONIQ 6 in the US after the 2026 model year, while the performance N will remain on sale.

#4797. How a Freak Flood Revealed the Gut-Brain Axis

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

“There is a tide in the affairs of men, which taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.” —William Shakespeare

In May 2000, the Canadian town of Walkerton was flooded after a heavy rain. The town’s water supply became contaminated with E. coli and Campylobacter jejuni. It was caused by overflow from a cow and chicken farm known to have problems containing their pathogens. Over two thousand of the five thousand townsfolk became seriously ill. Seven died. The town basically shut down. And then it was noticed that hundreds of these people, after recovering from their original infections, came down with IBS. They also became depressed.

Although E. coli was present in the water, C. jejuni arguably played a bigger role in the disaster. C. jejuni is sensitive to stomach acids, which quickly killed many of the microbes. But people who regularly took antacids had lower levels of acidity, allowing more of the C. jejuni to pass through. Those using proton-pump inhibitors were twice as likely to get sick from C. jejuni.

Although diminished, many of these pathogens still made it to the intestines. These bacteria were recently inside a cow or a chicken, so they were pretty much at home in the human gut. In cows and chickens, C. jejuni is a commensal. Why it goes berserk in a human gut is unclear, but C. jejuni is potent: It is the number-one cause of diarrhea in the United States, ahead of Salmonella and E. coli. The odds are good that you’ve had it at least once in your life.

In response to C. jejuni, special cells lining the intestines secreted serotonin, which increased peristalsis in anticipation of purging.

C. jejuni caused anxiety even without a full-blown infection. Cells lining the gut called neuropods detected the invasion, causing the nervous system to go on alert before the immune system kicked in. This was an early shot across the bow; the brain now knew something was up down below.

Some heroic microbes emerged to face down the C. jejuni, including Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species. They worked to outcompete and crowd out the C. jejuni, preventing them from sticking to the cells lining the gut. Ironically, those who had taken antibiotics recently had lost this microbial defense and they were hit harder by the C. jejuni.

Sadly, the city officials of Walkerton insisted that the water was safe, and people kept drinking it. The C. jejuni soon overwhelmed their microbial defenses, eating through the mucus lining the gut and leaving tender gut cells exposed to infection.

Once attached to a cell, C. jejuni makes a toxin that stops gut cells from dividing. Without division, gut cells can't renew themselves and when they die, the gut lining begins to leak. A leaky gut leads to inflammation. Sure enough, the citizens of Walkerton came down with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), along with its accompanying depression and anxiety.

Stephen Collins, a professor at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, took the two-hour drive to Walkerton to see if there was a way to snatch some useful research from the town's misery.

For eight years Collins followed this group of unlucky Canadians and found that many of them had suffered intractable IBS ever since their initial infection. Collins recognized this as post-infectious IBS, which was first seen in soldiers who had picked up dysentery during World War II. About one in eight cases of IBS starts this way. Collins discovered a significant association between IBS and the mental conditions of depression and anxiety.

Intriguingly, Collins found that people with pre-existing depression had double the risk of contracting IBS. This observation underlines the dual nature of the gut-brain dialogue. It creates a positive-feedback loop, a vicious cycle that can be hard to break.

The initial infection caused the immune system to move swiftly to eradicate the offending bacteria. But in some people, the immune response failed to wind down after eliminating the pathogens, leading to treatment-resistant IBS.

Collins was joined in the research project by Premysl Bercik, also of McMaster University. Bercik took fecal matter from IBS patients and transplanted it into mice. The mice subsequently developed anxiety-like behavior, demonstrating that gut microbiota can affect mental states and that, intriguingly, those states can be transferred from one animal to another. The idea that mental states could be transmitted via fecal transplant took most scientists by surprise.

In the wake of the disaster, Walkerton erected a waterfall commemorating the victims. But the people who got IBS and became depressed started an important conversation about how the gut is related to the brain. Today, their suffering is also memorialized by the astonishing revelations of the gut-brain axis.

John K. Marshall et al., “Eight Year Prognosis of Postinfectious Irritable Bowel Syndrome Following Waterborne Bacterial Dysentery,” Gut 59, no. 5 (May 1, 2010): 605–11, doi:10.1136/gut.2009.202234.

Wei, Li, Lasantha Ratnayake, Gabby Phillips, Chris C. McGuigan, Steve V. Morant, Robert W. Flynn, Isla S. Mackenzie, and Thomas M. MacDonald. “Acid Suppression Medications and Bacterial Gastroenteritis: A Population-Based Cohort Study.” British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, January 1, 2016, n/a-n/a. doi:10.1111/bcp.13205.

#4795. Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV

Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.

Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.

Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”

Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.

Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.

All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.

According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”

The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.

The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.

Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.

To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.

And for a mere 10-15% reduction in efficiency, our beautiful American suburbanites can Look Butch as they drive about town. Hopefully Toyota offers a package that attaches a shovel and some jerry cans to complete the image.

The bZ Woodland also adds off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and the ability to tow up to 3,500 lbs.

Other rugged upgrades include All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

#4794. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

For more information, Healthgrades’ Specialty Excellence Patient Advocate Center provides access to the information you need to make informed decisions about your care. This resource includes an overview of how Healthgrades picks award recipients, plus a list of the top U.S. hospitals for specialty care.

To be eligible for a Specialty Excellence Award, hospitals must receive a rating in the required procedures and conditions used to determine the award. Some awards are based on a single procedure, while others are based on a grouping of procedures. #4792. How Emotions Shape Our Impressions of Others

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

This post was co-authored with Rebecca Schlegel, Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Texas A&M University.

What do you think of when you hear the word stereotype? This term has become highly polarizing in today’s society. It probably brings to mind ideas like social justice; diversity, equity, and inclusion training; meritocracy; oppression; wokeness; and equity. You probably have emotions about these ideas, possibly strong ones, and have attitudes about what we should do as a society about these things. But what comes to mind is probably not what psychologists mean when they study stereotypes, and people are often surprised by the role of emotions in shaping what we think about others.

When viewed through a psychological lens, stereotypes are not good or bad. They are byproducts of how people think. The human mind operates by creating categories or “bins” and using those bins to collect related information. As children learn language, for example, they might create a bin called “dogs,” and place everything that is four-legged and furry into that bin. This leads to some common errors, such as children calling a cat a “dog” because it is four-legged and furry. Typically, these errors are corrected by others (a parent explains it is not a dog, but a cat), and the categories get adjusted as children learn what information goes in what bin. This structure is critical for functioning in the world—we can enter a new situation and know what to expect because we’ve been in similar situations before. Without the category of “dog,” we would have to treat every encounter with a dog as a new experience. With the category of “dog,” we have some idea of how the animal will behave and what we should and shouldn’t do when encountering a dog, and we can talk with other people about our experiences with dogs to share information. Overall, categories help us learn faster and function better.

We use this same categorization process to make sense of the many different types of people we encounter in the world. From an early age, we learn categories and place people into those categories. We learn some bins at very young ages, such as family versus stranger. As we grow and learn, the categories are adjusted based on correcting errors and greater experience. Placing people into those categories allows us to quickly respond—children learn to treat someone in the bin of “stranger” very differently than they treat someone in the bin of “family.”

Stereotypes refer to the information and beliefs we put in the bins we have learned for groups of people. Just as people might associate the bin of “dog” with concepts like loyal or energetic, people associate bins for groups of people with different concepts. For example, people may associate the category of “football player” with concepts like “strong.” At their root, stereotypes are mental shortcuts that people use to make sense of other people just as they do with other types of categories in the world. Creating the bins and putting information in the bins is just a feature of how our brain makes sense of a complicated world.

The challenge comes when we develop emotions about the bins we use. One person might associate the bin of “dog” with loyalty and develop good feelings about dogs, whereas another person might associate the bin of “dog” with aggression and develop negative feelings about them. In the same way, people attach good or bad feelings to bins for categories of people. This process—where an emotion is attached to a category or idea—is called attitude formation. The bin is no longer neutral—there is an emotional tag that changes how you interact with the members of that category. If the bin of “dogs” is attached to negative feelings or fear, you avoid dogs. Similarly, you are disposed to act differently toward categories of people associated with negative emotions versus groups you associate with positive emotions. These emotions can be powerful guides to behavior.

The beliefs we hold about groups of people and the emotional responses we have toward the groups are different concepts in psychology. In daily life, however, these things often go hand in hand and are influenced by the messages we receive about groups. Societal views of smoking and smokers in the United States are an excellent example of how stereotypes (and the emotions they evoke) develop and can shift. From the 1920s through the 1960s, smoking was associated with glamor and wealth. This was the result of marketing by companies and striking images of celebrities in movies, ads, and television. Smoking was not only socially acceptable; it was a good thing—part of being a productive and engaged member of society. The group “smokers” had become associated with positive beliefs and positive emotions.

As the health consequences of smoking behavior and the resulting economic impact became clear, government officials took steps to change public perceptions of smoking. They banned cigarette advertisements, promoted anti-smoking campaigns, and prohibited companies from using terms that suggested particular brands were safer or healthy. Many of the campaigns were graphic and evoked strong emotion, such as images of smokers with cigarette burns in their clothes and yellowed teeth, diseased lungs, or people in wheelchairs struggling to breathe. These messages were not just providing information to people about the health risks—they were actively attempting to shift the stereotypes of smoking and smokers. Over time, “smokers” became associated with negative emotions and beliefs, and were viewed as dangerous, irresponsible, selfish, unhealthy, and disgusting. They were banned from restaurants, airplanes, workplaces, campuses, and stores.

In current society, there is a high level of concern and attitudes about stereotypes and what we should do about them. Stereotypes have become a focus of political debate and calls to action. However, from a psychological perspective, stereotypes exist because they are a byproduct of how people learn, think, and navigate a complex social world, and they cannot be removed. But we can understand how messages through advertising, media, and other sources affect the impressions we form about other people. Understanding how our impressions are formed can help all of us make more intentional evaluations about other people based on our own experiences and our personal values.

#4790. The 8 Best Sweater Polos for Men, According to Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Your next best-dressed moment starts from the collar down.

I CONSIDER MYSELF the king of sweaters. I love a good collared shirt, so polos are my go-to in the spring and summer. But once fall and winter roll around, I’m all about sweaters. Even better: a sweater polo. It’s the perfect mashup that combines the collar and button placket of a classic polo with the knit construction of a sweater, giving you a little more texture and warmth than your standard cotton pique. The best sweater polos offer that same versatility. You can dress things up or lean super casual depending on the day and occasion. And not all have to be long-sleeved either.

Short-sleeve versions are also great for tropical vacations or layers under a blazer for the office. Either way, they’re an easy way to switch up your usual sweater rotation from the same ol’ crews or turtlenecks. The Men’s Health fashion crew and I have tried more than 30 over the last three years, paying close attention to fit, fabric, comfort, and versatility to find ones that deserve a spot in your closet.

For the past five years, I’ve tested more than 25 sweater polos, but Uniqlo is easily one of my favorites. It checks all the boxes when it comes to excellent quality, fit, versatility and what really seals the deal—affordability. At just $50, you’re getting a premium knit that could pass for something more expensive. It’s made from a cotton-blend yarn in a structured Milano rib knit that looks and feels more like woven cloth than a stretchy tee. This one feels dense yet comfortable on the skin. I especially love the buttonless, open V-neck collar, which gives some breathing room and makes the whole thing feel a little relaxed.

In terms of fit, it’s roomy through the chest and flexible through the arms without looking oversized. I’ve worn it with jeans and dressed it up with tailored trousers and loafers for dinner. Plus, it comes in plenty of colors that you can rotate between office days and the weekend. After more than three wash cycles, it’s held up nicely. Just be sure to toss it in a mesh laundry bag to keep the knit in good shape.

You don’t have to spend a fortune to get your hands on a good sweater polo. Check out this one from Coofandy. It’s one of the lighter knits that I’ve tested, so it’s wearable through all the seasons. Yes, even in the summertime when the temps stayed around 80 degrees, I didn’t break a sweat at the backyard party. The polyester fabric feels soft against the skin and has a little stretch, which makes it easy to move around in.

It also has a V-neck polo collar to give it that laid-back vibe, while the ribbed cuffs and hem pull everything in for a more fitted, body-contouring look. Styling-wise, you’ve got plenty of options. I’d wear it untucked with jeans or chinos for an everyday fit, but you can also tuck it in pants with a belt for a day on the golf course. This one is not machine washable, so I’d recommend taking a trip to the dry cleaners.

I love mixing different textures in my polo sweater collection, so things don’t start looking too plain. That’s when I add in pieces like Charles Tyrwhitt’s textured knit to give some depth and dimension to my outfit without going overboard with loud patterns or prints. It’s made from 100 percent cotton that’s been garment-washed for a softer, broken-in feel, so I’m not dealing with a stiff, scratchy sweater.

The midweight material is substantial enough to wear on its own during cooler days but breathable enough to layer under a jacket without feeling too bundled up. I’d wear the petrol-blue shade with cream trousers and brown suede loafers for a sharp office look, or pair it with dark denim and boots for dinner. I’ve washed it more than four times and haven’t seen it shrink or pill, but my advice is to let it air dry.

When my brain can’t function in the morning to put an outfit together, I just rely on Abercrombie’s knit. It’s made from 100 percent merino wool, which sounds like it might be a recipe for itchiness, but surprisingly, it feels soft and smooth against the skin. I also dig the classic three-button collar, which gives it a slightly dressier edge than your average crewneck. The fit is also a nice balance, with enough room in the chest and stomach, in case I wolfed down a burger.

Now, I will say that the wool can get a little toasty, especially if you’re moving around a lot. But if your office blasts AC like it’s the middle of Antarctica, you should be just fine. Styling-wise, I’d wear it with straight-leg jeans and sneakers for a casual Friday, or swap in chinos and loafers when I want to look a little more put-together. It only comes in neutrals, which should be easy to pair with anything in your wardrobe.

There’s something about cashmere that makes even the simplest outfit feel a little more luxurious. And if you’re going to invest in a cashmere sweater polo, Quince is a great place to start. This one is made from 100 percent Grade-A Mongolian cashmere, with fine fibers that give the knit an incredibly soft, smooth feel. The 12-gauge construction gives it a refined look without making it feel overly chunky, and the ribbed cuffs and hem help keep its shape. And when I don’t want to wear a dress shirt, this is a great alternative. Throw it on with tailored trousers and loafers for the office, or pair it with dark jeans and boots for dinner.

I’m a big fan of merino wool because it gives you the warmth of a sweater minus all the extra bulk. Banana Republic uses it for this polo, which is a solid option that can transition from the office straight to dinner. No matter how toasty a room gets, I’m never sweating in it. The fabric stays lightweight and breathable, and has enough warmth to come in handy when temperatures drop.

I also like that the fit is pretty straightforward, with slightly dropped shoulders and ribbed cuffs and hem that give it a relaxed but clean finish. The buttoned collar makes it feel a little dressier than your average knit, especially when paired with chinos or tailored trousers. And unlike some wool sweaters that require a trip to the dry cleaner, this one is machine washable, which is always a plus in my book.

Cos gave the classic sweater polo a completely different spin with a buttonless collar that sits closed rather than opening into the usual V-neck. It’s a subtle detail, but one that makes people take a second look at my outfit. This neckline creates a cleaner, more sophisticated look without being overly flashy. I’d pair it with wide-leg trousers and leather loafers for a sharp office fit, or throw it on with relaxed jeans and sneakers for the weekend.

I especially like this kind of silhouette for guys who prefer a minimalist wardrobe but still want something with a little personality. Now, at around $130, it’s definitely on the pricier side, especially when you can find sweater polos for half that amount. But I’d argue you’re paying for a design that’s a refreshing departure from the sweater polos you’re used to seeing, and chances are, you won’t spot five other guys wearing the same thing.

Not every sweater polo needs long sleeves, especially when you can rock one under a blazer. Take this retro-inspired short-sleeve style from Bonobos, which I can wear year-round. My favorite way to style it is under a structured blazer with tailored trousers. It’s dressy enough to skip the traditional button-down shirt, whether you’re heading to an important meeting or a cocktail reception.

It’s also a great piece to pack for vacation, especially if you’re traveling somewhere tropical and need something sharp for a resort dinner. In that case, ditch the blazer and pair it with linen pants or even shorts for a more laid-back look. Plus, the breathable cotton fabric won’t make scorching temps feel even more unbearable. I wore it on a recent trip to Cancún and didn’t break much of a sweat. Depending on your personal style, Bonobos offers this sweater polo in a variety of colors, prints, and textures, so there’s plenty to choose from.
