#4788. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4787. Tesla drops car referral rewards, now pays owners in FSD for referrals

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.

At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.

To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page. Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.

The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.

The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page. Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.

Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.

That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024, a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.

That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.

The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.

The only way I would ever pay for FSD is if Tesla covered full comprehensive insurance for my vehicle and accepted all liability. Otherwise, it's a gamble with my (and others') life.

That they seem to prioritize this sham service (Just call it Assisted Driving for honesty sake?) versus improving the cars or lowering prices, tells me enough not to look at Tesla for my next vehicle.

The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.

So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

#4785. A Forgotten Remedy for Depression

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Devon Frye

There’s growing concern about the risks of antidepressants, including side effects and withdrawal symptoms. Many people who are taking antidepressants are now turning to deprescribing resources, while others who are experiencing depression are wondering whether they should start taking antidepressants at all or if there’s another way.

But there’s one remedy that hasn’t gotten the attention it deserves: exercise.

In what follows, I’ll look at the surprising antidepressant effects of exercise, why it isn’t prescribed more widely, and a simple framework to help people get started.

One of the most astonishing findings in recent depression research is that exercise can be as effective as antidepressants, and some studies suggest it may be even more effective for mild to moderate depression. Millions of people have been prescribed powerful psychiatric drugs, often without being told that something as ordinary as walking, jogging, cycling, or strength training might provide comparable benefits.

The evidence has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Exercise ranks as one of the most effective known lifestyle interventions for depression. These include aerobic exercises, walking, jogging, strength training, and yoga. Intriguingly, evidence suggests that strength training is slightly more effective for women and younger adults, and yoga for men and older adults.

Exercise isn't just about shedding calories. It improves inflammation, metabolism, sleep, and the body's response to stress. These are precisely the factors that can go wrong in depression. But I think there's something deeper going on.

I've argued that depression may be a functional signal: our brain's way of telling us that something in our lives isn't going well and needs more attention. Sometimes the problem is a relationship, a job, or a life goal that no longer suits us. But sometimes the problem is the way we're living.

Humans evolved to move. Our ancestors spent much of their days walking, gathering food, carrying things, and engaging physically with the world. They didn't spend eight hours sitting in front of a computer, followed by another four hours staring at a smartphone. Yet that's how many of us live today.

Is it surprising that our bodies, and our minds, are protesting? Perhaps depression is telling us that something is wrong with the lives we've built for ourselves.

The evidence for the benefits of exercise is strong enough that a group of psychiatrists recently asked, in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, whether failing to prescribe exercise for depression could amount to “psychiatric malpractice.”

Part of the problem, they argue, is training. In one survey, 92 percent of mental health professionals said they'd received no formal training in prescribing exercise, and 41 percent said they never prescribe it at all.

Still, simply telling people to “be active” rarely works. People who struggle with depression need guidance and support.

For those for whom exercise is a real possibility, the same group offers a simple framework called FITT, which stands for frequency, intensity, time, and type. As a rule of thumb (and obviously to be adjusted for each person's physical health and other medical conditions):

But they also emphasize that less is better than none. Even one or two sessions a week, or 10 to 30 minutes at a time, can help.

Sometimes, what depression may be pointing to is precisely the mismatch between how we are designed to live and how we actually live. Exercise may be one way of answering its call.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THEY’VE BEEN CROPPING up everywhere. All over my social media feed, featured across men’s runway collections at Fashion Week, seen on Hollywood heartthrobs like Michael B. Jordan, and so forth. If you haven’t figured it out by now, I’m talking about the henley. This once-overlooked wardrobe staple has found new popularity, showing no signs of slowing down as it becomes one of fall’s most surprising menswear trends. And quite frankly, I’m here for it.

The henley hasn’t traditionally been the sexiest shirt in a guy’s wardrobe. For years, it’s been the tee you’d throw on for a lazy Sunday or wear underneath a flannel. But somewhere along the way, the fashion crowd decided it deserved another shot. Its roots go all the way back to 19th-century England, where it started as an undergarment before becoming a go-to for rowers in Henley-on-Thames, hence the name. Who would’ve thought a shirt with such humble beginnings would eventually become a fashion obsession on my Instagram timeline?

Cos Slim Ribbed Cotton Long-Sleeved Henley T-Shirt

Todd Snyder Lightweight Mini Waffle Henley

Cherry Los Angeles Waffle-Knit Cotton-Blend Henley T-Shirt

California Arts Murray Slim Long Sleeve Henley

Here’s what I love about the henley: It does more heavy lifting than your average T-shirt without trying to be anything fancy. You get the simplicity of a crewneck, the button placket of a polo, and just enough texture to make an otherwise basic outfit feel put-together. And while the classic cotton version is still very much in rotation, ribbed, waffle-knit, and thermal styles are giving guys even more ways to wear it. If you need further proof that the henley is having a moment, just take a peek at the runways. For Fall/Winter 2026, Paul Smith sent a model down the runway in a white henley tucked into wide-leg black trousers, while Isabel Marant took a more layered approach, pairing a light blue henley with a navy corduroy jacket.

I’m a firm believer that proportions can make or break an outfit, and the henley is no exception. My favorite way to wear one is with baggy jeans or relaxed trousers. The contrast between a fitted top and roomier bottoms creates a flattering silhouette. And if you’ve spent the past few months putting in work at the gym, a henley is one of the easiest ways to show off those gains without looking like you’re showing off. The closer fit naturally accentuates your chest, shoulders, and biceps, especially when you leave the top button or two undone. Just remember, there’s a fine line between fitted and too tight.

Whether you’re dressing one up with trousers and loafers or keeping things casual with loose jeans and boots, the henley proves that sometimes the most unexpected trends are the pieces we’ve had in our closets all along. And it’s about time this one received its flowers.

#4781. Can a CAPTCHA Make You Think About God?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

You have done it hundreds of times. A grid of blurry squares appears; you click the ones with traffic lights, and you move on. Nobody has ever asked what was going through your mind while you proved you were not a robot.

In a paper just published in Behavior Research Methods, my colleagues and I used that same task to bring religious ideas to people's minds. Then we checked whether it actually worked.

For about 20 years, psychologists have been asking whether reminding people of God makes them more honest or generous. In his 2013 book Big Gods, Ara Norenzayan argued that belief in a god who watches and punishes helped strangers cooperate once societies grew too large for neighbors to monitor each other. Dominic Johnson had been making a related case since 2004, with more weight on the fear of punishment than on being watched, a point he later expanded in his book God Is Watching You. If either version is right, even a short reminder of God should change behavior in the lab.

The problem is the reminder itself. In implicit priming, participants unscramble sentences containing words like “divine” or “spirit,” in the hope that religious thoughts become active without anyone noticing. These primes are often too weak to demonstrate activation. In explicit priming, participants write a few sentences about God. This works, but many participants can guess what the study is about, and some then behave the way they think a good person should.

The findings have been messy as a result. A 2016 meta-analysis by Azim Shariff and his colleagues concluded that religious priming increases prosocial behavior. But when Michiel van Elk and his colleagues reanalyzed the same data in 2015, two different bias-correction methods yielded different answers: One suggested the entire effect could be explained by publication bias; the other suggested a real effect remained. Their conclusion was that meta-analysis alone cannot settle the question, and that only large, preregistered studies can. A 2024 meta-analysis by Shariff's research group added another twist: The association between religious belief and prosocial behavior appears mostly in what people say about themselves, and much less in what they do.

And almost none of these primes had ever been tested to see whether they really make people think about religion. We assumed they did.

Fırat Şeker, a former master's student of mine who is now pursuing his Ph.D. at UMass Amherst, and Ensar Acem, one of my current Ph.D. students and the manager of our MINT Lab at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, co-led a project to change this.

The idea was to hide the prime inside something people see every day. We built two versions.

In the grid version, participants saw a photo of an open book divided into 16 squares. A short phrase sat in one corner: “God sees,” “God punishes,” “God rewards,” or “God forgives.” The control group saw “He runs” in the same spot. Everyone was told to select the squares with no readable text, just as in an ordinary CAPTCHA.

In the keyword version, participants saw a picture of a Bible and had to pick the word that best described it. The right answer was “sacred,” hidden among options like “train,” “bed,” and “pencil.” The control group saw a photo of a table and had to pick “table” in the same way.

Then came the test. In a preregistered study of 2,770 American Christians, all participants completed a word-completion task. Participants saw fragments such as “f a i _ _” and filled in the blank, which could become “faith” or “faint.” Count the religious words people produce, and you have a behavioral measure of how easily religious thoughts come to mind. After that, participants played a standard dictator game, deciding how much of a small sum to share with a stranger. At the end, we asked them what they thought the study was about.

The explicit prime produced the strongest effect, as expected. But 11 percent of those participants correctly guessed the study's purpose.

The keyword version worked. When people had to find the word “sacred” under a picture of a Bible, they later produced more religious words than the control group did, and the same was true for the versions that pointed to a rewarding or a forgiving God. The version that pointed to a punishing God did not raise religious thoughts in general, but it did raise thoughts about sin and punishment specifically. Only 6 percent of these participants guessed what the study was about. The grid version did not work at all. We told people to select the squares without text, so they barely processed the sentence. A prime can be subtle, but it still needs a few seconds of attention.

Generosity did not change under any prime, including the explicit one. The experimental record here is mixed. In 2018, Joseph Billingsley and his colleagues found that an explicit prime increased giving in a dictator game while an implicit prime did not, and Cristina Gomes and Michael McCullough had found no effect of implicit priming on the same game in 2015. The meta-analytic picture depends on how one corrects for publication bias, as van Elk and his colleagues showed. So a null result is not out of line with what others have found. There is also a design reason. Norenzayan’s point in Big Gods was that religion works when it is in the situation, at the moment a person decides. In our study, the word-completion task came between the prime and the game, so by the time people chose how much to give, the reminder may already have faded. But when a religious prime fails to affect behavior in future studies, researchers can now rule out the most boring explanation: that the prime never reached anyone in the first place.

There is now a tested, low-suspicion method for activating religious thoughts in online studies. It has separate primes for punishing, rewarding, and forgiving images of God. That separation matters. Researchers disagree about whether it is the feeling of being watched or the fear of punishment that makes religious people behave better, and until now there was no clean way to pull the two apart. The materials and data are freely available on OSF.

Almost 10 years ago, Hasan G. Bahçekapili and I argued in Religion, Brain and Behavior that the question “Is religion necessary for morality?” has an easy answer: no, since plenty of people are moral without any religious belief. The harder question, and the one that remains unsolved, is how religion transforms morality once it enters the picture, in our evolutionary past, in history, and in the life of a single person. One reason it stayed unsolved is that we could not trust our own manipulations. Some questions that were put aside as unanswerable may only have been waiting for better tools. The same trick should also work outside religion, for anything that fits in the corner of a picture.

Everyone has heard of the replication crisis in psychology. Its sibling, the validity crisis, gets much less attention. In 2021, David Chester and Emily Lasko reviewed the experimental manipulations used in social psychology and found that most had never been tested to see whether they changed what they were supposed to change. A result can replicate perfectly and still be about nothing in particular.

Validation studies are not glamorous and rarely make the news. But before we ask whether God makes people good, we need to be sure that we have actually made them think about God. The field needs many more studies like this one, and far fewer assumptions.

Bahçekapili, H. G., & Yilmaz, O. (2017). Is religion necessary for morality? Religion, Brain & Behavior, 7(4), 279–281. https://doi.org/10.1080/2153599X.2016.1249924

Billingsley, J., Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2018). Implicit and explicit influences of religious cognition on Dictator Game transfers. Royal Society Open Science, 5(8), 170238. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.170238

Chester, D. S., & Lasko, E. N. (2021). Construct validation of experimental manipulations in social psychology: Current practices and recommendations for the future. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 16(2), 377–395. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691620950684

Johnson, D., & Krüger, O. (2004). The good of wrath: Supernatural punishment and the evolution of cooperation. Political Theology, 5(2), 159–176. https://doi.org/10.1558/poth.2004.5.2.159

Johnson, D. (2015). God Is Watching You: How the Fear of God Makes Us Human. Oxford University Press.

Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2015). The effects of implicit religious primes on dictator game allocations: A preregistered replication experiment. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), e94–e104. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000027

Kelly, J. M., Kramer, S. R., & Shariff, A. F. (2024). Religiosity predicts prosociality, especially when measured by self-report: A meta-analysis of nearly 60 years of research. Psychological Bulletin, 150(3), 284–318. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000413

Norenzayan, A. (2013). Big Gods: How Religion Transformed Cooperation and Conflict. Princeton University Press.

Shariff, A. F., Willard, A. K., Andersen, T., & Norenzayan, A. (2016). Religious priming: A meta-analysis with a focus on prosociality. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 20(1), 27–48. https://doi.org/10.1177/1088868314568811

Şeker, F., Acem, E., Vurgun, R., Dogruyol, B., Isler, O., & Yilmaz, O. (2026). Divine verification: Introducing a CAPTCHA-based religious priming technique. Behavior Research Methods, 58, 316. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03147-1

van Elk, M., Matzke, D., Gronau, Q. F., Guan, M., Vandekerckhove, J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2015). Meta-analyses are no substitute for registered replications: A skeptical perspective on religious priming. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, Article 1365. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01365

#4779. BYD reveals a flashy new feature on its upcoming luxury EV

BYD is moving upmarket with its new flagship EV, featuring suicide doors, a gemstone grille, and possibly solid-state batteries.

Yangwang is like BMW’s Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach, sitting at the very top of BYD’s brand hierarchy.

The ultra-luxury brand offers BYD’s most high-end and technically advanced vehicles, including the U7 sedan, the U8, a hardcore off-road SUV, and the U9, an electric supercar.

Yangwang vehicles have previously debuted with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including its quad-motor e4 platform (delivering over 1,300 hp), its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its DiSus-X intelligent body control system.

Its next model will push further into the elite segment. After BYD revealed the name of its new flagship executive sedan earlier this week, the Yangwang Altior, the company has released several new details ahead of its official debut.

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing confirmed on Friday that the new Yangwang Altior will feature suicide doors, a first for a BYD model.

The new door design swings open nearly 90 degrees, Hu said, creating a dramatic, wide-open entrance.

Hu also posted a preview of the vehicle’s front fascia, complete with a dot-matrix Gemstrone grille and crystal-inspired headlights.

BYD has not confirmed many details, but the ultra-luxury sedan is expected to be about 5,500 mm (216″) in length.

Images of the disguised vehicle released last month show a similar shape and size to the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom.

HU said last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.

BYD has not revealed an official date, but according to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD aims to unveil the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.

The Yangwang Altrio will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said.

In one image, the vehicle was charging at a BYD Flash Charge station, suggesting it will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology.

There are companies showcasing flying cars designed specifically for circus-style shows, while others are launching solid-state batteries that can recharge in five minutes.

#4777. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4776. Narrative and Illness: The Autobiographical Stories We Tell Matter

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Humans love stories. From oral storytelling to novels to movies and television—we make sense of our world through narrative. Through stories, we seek to understand ourselves and be understood by others. Stories are especially important in identity construction. That is, we define ourselves in large part by the narrative we tell about who we are. As identity is profoundly changed by illness, how do we work with our narrative to reflect this shift?

For most people, illness is a “biographical disruption.” It’s an unexpected and often devastating event that blows up life as we’ve known it. We become acquainted with pain, fear, loneliness, and limitations. The people we were before illness could count on our bodies to work. The people we were before illness understood suffering as an abstract concept rather than as a lived experience. The people we were before illness had freedom in moving through the world that we took entirely for granted.

When illness strikes, we experience deep grief. We mourn for the things we have lost, especially our pre-illness identity. The grief is necessary, as we can never be who we once were. As we go through the grief process, we have to make a narrative decision: Is illness the end of our story, or is there a way our story can continue?

In their article “Volition as Narrative: Understanding Motivation in Chronic Illness,” Helfrich, Kielhofner, & Mattingly (1994) describe two people whose lives have been interrupted by serious illness. One individual continues to fight for his lifelong dream of being a reporter. He’s had to reconceptualize what this will look like. While he may never write for a prestigious national publication, he finds ways to continue reporting for smaller outlets, pivoting as needed. He says, “[P]eople who don’t get sick make [long-term] plans. Every plan that I’ve made has eventually been defeated and I’ve had to shift to another subplan.” But he keeps shifting, as many times as he needs to. He keeps writing more chapters of his life story.

The other case study in the article describes a woman who has not been able to make a meaningful life for herself post-illness. She says, “I feel like I got cheated out of my life.” In contrast to the first case study, her story ended with illness. No further chapters were written.

One important narrative concept is “character.” How often do we read or watch a story and remark on the characters presented? While the events that occur in a story are certainly important, the intersection of plot with character is what makes stories so meaningful. In the article discussed above, for example, the reporter is a richly developed character. He is smart, determined, and resourceful. He is resilient. His sense of himself as a character with these traits enables him to meet the plot twist in his story with the strengths he believes himself to possess.

If I were working with the woman in the article, I’d want to get a sense of who she imagines herself to be as a character in her own life story. I’m guessing she may never have thought about herself in this way. I would ask her to tell me what she was like as a kid: What did she enjoy playing? Who did she enjoy playing with? I would ask her to tell me what she wanted for herself prior to illness and what she hopes for herself now. I would ask her to tell me what traits she values in herself and in others. I would ask her to flesh out for me who she is as a character in her own story. Undoubtedly, we would discover character traits we could build upon, strengths that might guide her as she imagines continuing her narration post-illness.

Another important narrative concept is “other characters.” Stories typically involve characters interacting with other characters. In the article, the reporter mentions the support his mother gave him. By contrast, the woman speaks of an interaction with a doctor in which he told her that her illness would prevent her from ever finishing college. As in novels and films, other people are tremendously important in our life stories. In our own stories, who are the characters that support us, that help us along the way? Who are the characters who cut us down and make our lives feel smaller and harder? How can we invite in supportive characters while minimizing the damage done by non-supportive characters?

“Narratives are created between people” (Ellis-Hill, Payne, & Ward, 2008). A novel has readers. A movie has watchers. A story has listeners. We create stories because we want to be seen and understood. We listen to stories because we want to see and understand. What is the story you want to tell about your life? Who do you want to listen?

If you’ve never thought about your life story, or if your life story needs a rewrite, therapy is a great place to do this work. Like an editor, therapists can often see elements of a story that the writer can’t. We can help you identify threads of meaning that run through your story (themes), and we can help you view your story in different ways (perspectives). Most importantly, we can help you with the chapter you are writing right now, in the present. What do you want this chapter to look like? Who can you imagine yourself to be in these unchosen circumstances? It’s your story: What are you going to write?

Ellis-Hill, C., Payne, S., & Ward, C. (2008). Using stroke to explore the life thread model: an alternative approach to understanding rehabilitation following an acquired disability. Disability and Rehabilitation, 30(2), 150–159.

Helfrich, C., Kielhofner, G., & Mattingly, C. (1994). Volition as narrative: Understanding motivation in chronic illness. American Journal of Occupational Therapy, 48(4), 311–317.

#4773. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

#4771. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4769. Beyond 'Forgive and Forget': 5 Practical Relationship Habits

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

In an era dominated by relationship burnout and hyper-individualism, many couples find themselves trapped in endless cycles of friction and emotional distance. Breaking free requires adopting habits that run counter to modern culture. Here are some counterintuitive relationship habits you could consider adopting or adapting to fit the unique rhythm and idiosyncrasies of your (current or future) intimate relationship.

Life is a process of displacement. When you are born, you immediately become #1. As long as you are single, you remain #1—it’s still about you and your freedom.

When you get married, you become #2. You have to learn to put your spouse first (without compromising your deeply held values—that’s why choosing the right person is the most important decision you’ll ever make) if you want the marriage to work.

When you have a child, you become #3. By the time you become a grandparent, you’re lucky if you’re still in the Top 10.

While it sounds like you become weaker, it’s the opposite: You become stronger. While it sounds like you become a follower, it’s, again, the opposite: This is true leadership. The front-stage star is not a leader, but a showman—not the director, but an actor.

The true leader is the one you don’t see, the back-stage architect whose undying devotion enables the unfolding drama, which involves many, to captivate and enthrall, night after night.

Twenty-five years ago, I was wrestling with my inner demons about commitment and went on a walk along the Potomac River outside of Washington, DC, with a close family friend who had been married to his wife for more than 40 years.

“How have you managed being married for so long?” I asked him.

Robert looked at the turbulent rapids and thought for a while. Then he said, “The best advice I ever received was from my aunt, while I was fixing my tuxedo just before Charlene and I were married.”

“She said, ‘Robert, always remember this: Whatever Charlene does, just give. No matter what happens, always give. And the two of you will be fine.’”

I’ll pass on Robert’s aunt’s sage advice: Just give. No matter what. It’s your only power. You control how, when, and what to give.

What you receive, on the other hand, is completely out of your control. Yet the more and better you give, the more love will also come in your direction.

In other words, let things go. There are two things you do in life: You choose how you want to live, and you live with what you choose.

You chose a long-term commitment to this person, which means letting lots of things (but not everything) go. Consider that the opposite of forgiveness is resentment. A word derived from the Latin roots re (again) and sentire (to feel), resentment is to feel anger again and again until you become paralyzed.

Forgiveness is a better option: while resentment paralyzes, forgiveness liberates.

As children, we’re often told by adults—generally with good intentions—to “forgive and forget.” To forget, however, may not be the best idea.

If you fall into a ditch, the last thing you want to do is forget the location of the ditch. Such a strategy may result in your falling in again.

A better way to approach forgiveness is to acknowledge what the other person did, file it away, give for the other person to yourself, and then let it go. This approach need not include your tolerating the same behavior again.

Forgiveness, in fact, does not necessarily lead to a continued relationship. In many cases, forgiveness enables you to detach yourself from the relationship, not only physically but also emotionally and psychologically.

Importantly, while trust binds, forgiveness releases. While forgiveness is needed for personal development, trust is needed for relational development.

Trust is not necessarily an evolutionary adaptive behavior, as it can lead to more harmful behavior from the other person. A man can apologize to his wife for an affair, for example, regain her trust, and then continue to cheat on her afterward.

While trusting a specific person whom you feel has harmed you is not necessary for your evolution as a human being, forgiving them is. Forgiveness is one of your most critical attributes because until you let go of your suffering, you don’t let it recede from the present and into the past.

Until you forgive and then learn to love any person in your life, you remain trapped in a drama with them. You remain on their stage, entangled in an invisible thread that binds you to them.

You may be acting out the drama with the surrogates you bring into your life to replace them, but you are still cast in the role. This is how love liberates, how love sets you free.

The more you are able to take this cognitive step toward understanding and respecting innate differences that will always be beyond your control, the more inner peace and happiness you will invite into your life.

If you are like most of us, you probably have not yet made this transformative decision. You have likely spent most of your life preoccupied with the comings and goings and machinations and preferences of the other characters in your story—including and especially your partner—instead of seeing them as they are: as other human beings who enter and exit your stage throughout your life.

How can you accept yourself and others as you and they are while also retaining your optimism about what you and they can become?

#4768. Speeders just got lucky: the new Chevy police Silverado is NOT electric

Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.

If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric.

Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.

A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue.

I don’t know why anyone would use a truck as a persuit vehicle? It seems reckless inefficient and ineffective.

Guess we are on the topic of us policing…

#4766. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4765. The Benefits of Having an Older Sibling During Adolescence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Adolescence is an important time when young people seek independence from their parents, focusing on friends and romantic partners and figuring out who they want to be. As teens navigate these important developmental tasks, they will learn and grow with the help of others. For adolescents with an older sibling, that sibling can be an important, trusted family resource who helps guide them during this developmental period.

While siblings do spend less time together during adolescence, their relationship remains important and influential for youths' social, emotional, and cognitive development. In fact, adolescents report sharing and discussing personal information and thoughts with their siblings daily. Although older siblings are not always a positive influence, they can play a beneficial role in the lives of younger siblings during adolescence.

In the United States, most siblings are about two years apart in age, creating likely similarities in their life experiences. These similarities, along with siblings’ shared family history and special understanding of one another, can make an older sibling an ideal resource during adolescence. A sibling can also provide an alternative source of support for youth who may not feel comfortable talking to their parents or need a different perspective.

Teens may also seek out their older siblings as relatable confidants, perhaps using them as a sounding board before approaching their parents or other adults. Adolescents may enjoy the back-and-forth conversation with their sibling more than top-down pressure from parents. Reflecting this trust, research shows that adolescent siblings frequently talk about their daily activities, media use, nonfamilial relationships, academics, and future plans.

During adolescence, sibling support is often mutual, especially when navigating family matters. However, older siblings generally have more influence on younger siblings than vice versa, often adopting a teacher or mentor role even if they are only a few years older. Younger siblings often admire and look up to their older siblings. This status typically happens because of birth order and age: Older siblings are likely to face social situations with peers and romantic partners, encounter academic challenges and classes, and make decisions about future plans before their younger siblings.

Does it matter if an adolescent has an older brother or sister? The findings are mixed, with some studies showing no effect. Other studies show that younger siblings receive more guidance and support from same-sex rather than opposite-sex older siblings. This is thought to happen because same-sex siblings share greater similarities and relate to each other more easily. Additionally, older sisters are often close confidants and mentors for younger sisters and provide more advice than older brothers do. For example, one study found that older sisters give younger sisters specific instructions and information about dating and romantic relationships.

Older siblings can influence adolescent younger siblings in several ways, including by guiding them through direct instruction and encouragement or by providing information and advice. Another way older siblings influence younger siblings is by serving as role models. By watching their older siblings’ activities, choices, and subsequent consequences, younger siblings learn from them.

Older brothers and sisters are invaluable guides promoting positive development for their less experienced younger siblings in a variety of areas, including dating and peer relationships, body image, and prosocial skills like empathy. One study showed that older siblings shape adolescents’ social skills and their athletic and artistic interests, particularly when older siblings excelled in those areas. Other work found that how much adolescents discussed extracurricular activities, media, and academics with their older siblings was linked to their success in friendships, sports, and school.

Parents can encourage strong, loving sibling relationships in which older siblings serve as positive role models and resources for younger siblings during adolescence through the following suggestions:

Tucker, C. J., & Winzeler, A. (2007). Adolescent siblings’ daily discussions: Connections to perceived academic, athletic, and peer competency. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 17(1), 145–152. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1532-7795.2007.00515.x

Whiteman, S. D., & Christiansen, A. (2008). Processes of sibling influence in adolescence: Individual and family correlates. Family Relations, 57(1), 24–34. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1741-3729.2007.00480.x
